https://daryo.uz/en/2026/10/15/uzbekista.body: Uzbekistan Uzbekistan to provide state-funded lawyers to child victims and witnesses of violence Children who are victims or witnesses of violence in Uzbekistan will be entitled to state-funded legal assistance, including in criminal cases involving sexual violence, under a law signed by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev that also strengthens safeguards during investigations and court proceedings. Yesterday, 16:17 1 min read 128 views 0 comments 0 Source: Daryo Children who are victims or witnesses of violence in Uzbekistan will be entitled to state-funded legal assistance, including in criminal cases involving sexual violence, under a law signed by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. The law amends the legislation on state-funded legal aid, granting children the right to receive legal assistance from the moment they become involved in relevant procedural actions. Under amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code, lawyers providing state-funded legal assistance must participate in criminal cases involving sexual violence against minors to protect the interests of child victims and witnesses. The law also requires a representative of the guardianship and trusteeship authority to participate in all investigative and court proceedings when a minor is allegedly subjected to a crime by their parents, adoptive parents, guardians, trustees or other relatives. In addition, educational organizations will be allowed to terminate employment contracts with employees who have been held legally liable for committing violence against children. The law will enter into force on the date of its official publication. The legislation also introduces stricter penalties for certain sexual crimes against children under the age of 14. Under Parts Four of Articles 118 and 119 of the Criminal Code, offenders face 15 to 25 years in prison or life imprisonment. The amendments aim to strengthen safeguards for children affected by violence and improve their access to legal protection throughout criminal proceedings. The accredited media outlets include: Print publications — 19 Television and radio broadcasters — 22 Radio stations — 13 Online media outlets — 27. Information on advertising rates and placement terms will be published on the CEC website in the «Media Accreditation for Elections» section. The CEC reminded accredited media outlets that they are required by law to provide objective and accurate coverage of candidates’ election campaigns. The accreditation process was conducted through an automated information system. The presidential election in Kyrgyzstan is scheduled for January 27, 2027.

https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatch.body: Then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro looks on as he addresses the media at Miraflores Palace, in Caracas, Venezuela August 2, 2024. (Leonardo Fernandez Viloria via Reuters Connect) NEW YORK—Today, in a federal courthouse in Manhattan, Judge Alvin Hellerstein formally presented a charge of conspiracy to commit torture against Nicolás Maduro, the former dictator of Venezuela, and his wife Cilia Flores. The charge, to which both pled not guilty, has been added to the existing charges of narcoterrorism, drug trafficking, and weapons offenses against the defendants, whose trial is scheduled to begin in June 2027. The torture allegations include the use of state repression against political opponents and perceived dissidents in Venezuela, including at least three Americans, and form part of the charges in a superseding indictment unsealed by the US Department of Justice on October 8. The conspiracy to commit torture charge is significant for several reasons. Torture has a widely recognized definition , which is accepted by almost all United Nations (UN) member states. Torture is prohibited under international law, including by the UN Convention Against Torture , to which the United States and Venezuela are parties. Unlike the previous charges against Maduro, which center on alleged international drug trafficking and related weapons offenses, the new charge directly addresses the alleged use of state repression to quash political dissent in Venezuela—which international institutions have been documenting and reporting on for more than a decade, but with little prospect for redress. Because US federal law expressly provides for extraterritorial jurisdiction over torture committed abroad when the alleged offender is present in the United States, the new charge creates a potential and rare avenue for criminal accountability for acts of torture allegedly committed in Venezuela. What has happened in the case so far While efforts to hold Maduro accountable have come to a head only this year, the case against him has been long in the making. The indictment against Maduro and members of his inner circle was unsealed in 2020 . It alleged a wide-ranging drug trafficking operation aided by guerrilla groups and spanning multiple countries, dating back to 1999. In recent years, various co-conspirators pled guilty after extradition or surrender . As for Flores, she was first charged with drug trafficking and weapons offenses in December 2025. To date, the core allegations revolve around Maduro and Flores weaponizing parts of Venezuela’s law enforcement, the military, and the judiciary to protect a system of repression and corruption that allowed the couple and their inner circle to profit from drug trafficking and the theft of public funds. Following the US military capture of Maduro and Flores in January of this year, a superseding indictment was unsealed. The physical presence of Maduro and Flores in a US federal courtroom, which had initially seemed improbable, is now a reality. The prosecution can therefore proceed with the defendants in the dock. New York City police officers stand outside the Daniel Patrick Moynihan United States Courthouse where ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores faced a new indictment accusing them of torturing political opponents and US citizens to retain their grip on power, in New York City, US, October 15, 2026. (Eduardo Munoz via Reuters Connect) Torture charges are added In the superseding indictment unsealed by the Department of Justice on October 8, a count alleging “conspiracy to commit torture” was added to the charges against Maduro and Flores. This new count was brought under the US extraterritorial federal torture statute, Section 2340A of Title 18 of the United States Code. The indictment notes that in an effort “[t]o undermine Venezuelan democracy and entrench themselves in power,” Maduro and Flores “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens.” The indictment also details the types of torture allegedly used during their rule, including “electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells,” as well as psychological torture “such as threats to harm and kill victims’ families, including children.” In one grim example, prosecutors allege that Maduro caused the death of a Venezuelan opposition figure. In 2018, the now-deceased dissident had returned to Venezuela after attending the UN General Assembly in New York. Maduro’s forces arrested him and transferred him to the headquarters of Venezuela’s intelligence agency, where he was ordered to be tortured. Just three days after his arrest, Venezuelan authorities reported that the man had jumped to his death from the tenth floor of the facility. The indictment also alleges that Maduro and Flores tortured three unnamed US citizens. Dozens of Americans were wrongly detained during Maduro’s time in office. Upon release, many have recounted the torture they faced behind bars in media interviews and in civil lawsuits for damages. One potentially important figure in the case is former Venezuelan general Hugo Carvajal, who was arrested in Spain in 2021, extradited to the United States, and then pled guilty last year to drug trafficking charges. He led Venezuela’s military intelligence agency, previously known as the Dirección de Inteligencia Militar (DIM), for close to a decade under the rule of Hugo Chávez, Maduro’s predecessor. The revised indictment repeatedly mentions the involvement of the successor organization to the DIM, the Dirección General de Contrainteligencia Militar (DGCIM), in alleged acts of torture. While the testimony of victims is critical in establishing the responsibility of perpetrators in criminal trials, prosecutors often rely on insider witnesses to establish the chain of command or speak to the structures and networks that substantiate a conspiracy charge. If Carvajal testifies against Maduro , his statement could be key. Closing the impunity gap for Venezuelans The torture charges represent an important step forward in securing accountability for Venezuelans, for whom justice pathways so far have been quite limited. Since 2014, Venezuelan state forces led by Maduro have carried out waves of repression and violence against civilians. Following its establishment by the UN Human Rights Council in 2019, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (FFM) has published multiple reports detailing how Maduro-led forces committed crimes against humanity in Venezuela, including extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary detentions, and torture. Key to this repression is the role of the colectivos —pro-regime armed civilian groups tasked with repressing protests and political dissent and notorious for their brutality. Maduro’s human rights violations and atrocity crimes have received widespread condemnation by the UN , regional bodies in Latin America and Europe , countries around the world, and leading civil society organizations. Much of this is recounted in the unsealed indictment containing the torture charge. Despite the extensive documentation of the Maduro regime’s crimes, justice efforts have been halting. The International Criminal Court launched a preliminary examination into Maduro’s crimes in February 2018 and an investigation in November 2021, but this process has not yet resulted in any arrest warrants for Maduro or his regime officials. Argentina took the bold step of issuing arrest warrants in September 2024 for Maduro and other regime officials for crimes against humanity, but he remained at large. With Maduro and Flores now in US custody, and co-conspirators in the indictment potentially cooperating with US authorities, prosecutors may have a chance to hold Maduro and Flores to account

https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/society/.body: Home Azerbaijan Society Azerbaijan adds AI principle to journalists’ code of ethical conduct Society News 16 October 2026 11:37 (UTC +04:00) Humay Aghajanova Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. A principle regarding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) has been added to the Code of Ethical Conduct for Azerbaijani Journalists, the Press Council member Mushfig Alasgarli said at the 9th Congress of Azerbaijani Journalists in Baku on Friday, Trend ’s correspondent reports from the event. He noted that, according to the proposal, media entities should adopt internal documents establishing rules for the use of AI systems within their newsrooms. "Under the new principles, the use of AI systems mustn't replace a journalist's initiative and judgment, editorial independence, or human oversight. Before publishing material produced with the aid of AI, a human journalist must verify its content, factual accuracy, and sources. The journalist and the editorial office bear personal responsibility for the published material. Furthermore, transparency must be ensured to keep the audience accurately informed. Any content, such as photos, audio, or video, generated by AI that could potentially mislead the audience must be appropriately labeled, and the public must be informed about its origin," he added. The 9th Congress of Azerbaijani Journalists is being held at the Rashid Behbudov Song Theatre. A total of 225 delegates have confirmed their participation in the congress. Candidates for membership on the Press Council’s Board of Directors have been determined based on nomination forms submitted by organizations that are members of the Press Council. Among the current members of the Board of Directors, Rashad Majid, Aflatun Amashov, Gulu Maharramli, Umud Rahimoghlu, Aydin Guliyev, Rauf Arifoghlu, Elchin Mirzabayli, Vusala Mahirgizi, Agil Alasgar, Jeyhun Musaoghlu, Algish Musayev, Akif Ashirli, and Yadigar Mammadli have requested not to include their names on the ballot. Consequently, changes are expected for 13 of the 23 seats on the Press Council’s Board of Directors. https://www.spot.uz/en/2026/10/15/gas-im.body: An explosion was recently reported on the Central Asia-Center gas pipeline, which carries Russian gas to Uzbekistan. Photo: Issiqlikta’minoti Russian gas supplies to Uzbekistan continue in line with contractual obligations despite an explosion on the Central Asia-Center main gas pipeline in Russia, representatives of the Ministry of Energy and the Ministry of Economy and Finance said at a press conference on October 14 dedicated to energy tariff reform. “There is an intergovernmental agreement [with Russia] under which all parties fulfil their obligations on time,” a Ministry of Energy representative said in response to a question about the incident’s impact on gas supplies to Uzbekistan. Deputy Economy and Finance Minister Khurshed Mustafayev, who oversees the oil and gas sector, also said there were “no problems with [Russian gas] supplies”. “Supplies are being delivered on time in accordance with the terms of the contract signed between the two companies,” he said. On October 13, Kommersant reported an explosion on a gas pipeline near the village of Volchkovo in Russia’s Penza Region. The incident triggered intense flames, with the fire reaching around 70 metres in height. Authorities said the pipeline was promptly shut off. No deaths or injuries were reported. Advertising on Spot The Central Asia-Center pipeline is part of a roughly 5,000-km transport system connecting gas fields in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan with Russia and European consumers. In the first eight months of 2026, imports of natural and liquefied gas from Russia and Turkmenistan rose by 15.2% year-on-year to $1.21 billion. Of this amount, $124.3 million accounted for liquefied petroleum gas (propane), purchases of which increased 3.5 times. In August, imports of natural and liquefied gas totalled $206.1 million in value, up from $38.3 million in July. https://www.azernews.az/nation/265697.ht.body: President Ilham Aliyev received newly appointed Georgian ambassador to Azerbaijan [PHOTOS] 16 October 2026 13:30 (UTC+04:00) AzerNEWS Staff Read more On October 16, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev received George Zakarashvili, the newly appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Georgia to Azerbaijan. The ambassador presented his credentials to President Ilham Aliyev. President Ilham Aliyev fondly recalled his state visit to Georgia in April and the hospitality extended to him during the visit. Noting that Azerbaijan-Georgia relations have a rich history and a promising future, the head of state highlighted the successful development of friendly ties and strategic partnership between the two independent states, as well as the fraternal ties between their peoples. President Ilham Aliyev wished the ambassador success in his diplomatic mission. Expressing his gratitude for the reception, George Zakarashvili said that he felt greatly honored to be appointed ambassador to brotherly Azerbaijan and to meet with the head of state. He described the two countries as strategic partners and emphasized the close ties between their peoples. He underlined that, during his tenure, he would spare no effort to further strengthen the long-standing cooperation between Azerbaijan and Georgia. During the meeting, the sides welcomed the development of bilateral political relations and discussed cooperation in the fields of economy and trade, energy security, transport, communications, and other areas. They also discussed joint projects implemented by the two countries in the energy and transport sectors, noting their significance not only for the region but also globally. https://www.azernews.az/nation/265663.ht.body: Azerbaijan's Parliament warns of coordinated hybrid attacks against country 16 October 2026 10:45 (UTC+04:00) AzerNEWS Staff Read more Azerbaijan's emergence as a middle power under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev, its assertive foreign policy, growing international standing, contribution to global energy security, strategic importance in regional transit corridors, and domestic political and economic stability have significantly increased the scale of hybrid attacks against the country by foreign actors. These assessments were included in a statement issued by the Azerbaijani parliament's Temporary Commission on Foreign Interference and Hybrid Threats in connection with hybrid attacks targeting Azerbaijan. The statement reads: “Against the backdrop of ongoing wars and tensions in our region, the Republic of Azerbaijan, widely regarded as an island of stability, has recently faced religious and ideological provocations, coordinated information operations, and cyberattacks on an unprecedented scale and in a synchronized manner. “Under the pretext of promoting various freedoms, our people's centuries-old national, spiritual, and multicultural values, as well as their religious beliefs, are being targeted. Harmful activities are being used to undermine society's understanding of truth and present foreign ideologies to our people as the right path. “Investigations conducted jointly with the relevant state authorities have established that influence operations, cyberattacks, and attempts to carry out terrorist acts and sabotage are aimed at manipulating public opinion, creating polarization within society, and undermining trust in state institutions. These activities are conducted through agents of influence and clandestine organizations operating both inside and outside the country. In the digital sphere, they involve hacker groups, foreign media outlets, genuine and fake accounts, and bots. “We must express our regret that forces hostile to Azerbaijan, operating in friendly and neighboring countries, are injecting disinformation into digital platforms through channels that appear independent. Their objective is to create divisions along ethnic, religious, and political lines within society. They seek to sow discord within the country, turn citizens with differing views against one another, incite violence, and weaken our state from within. “Actors behind hybrid threats use a method known as ‘computational propaganda’ to confuse public opinion and deepen social fragmentation. They encourage people to actively seek out false information that supports their existing views in the media and on social networks, believe it, and spread it among others. “Algorithm-driven content distribution creates ‘echo chambers,’ exposing users primarily to information that reinforces their existing beliefs, opinions, and worldviews. Through the algorithms used by digital platforms, posts designed to provoke emotional reactions among our citizens are disseminated to large audiences. “Furthermore, the mechanism known as ‘filter bubbles’ ensures that harmful content reaches audiences already susceptible to it and previously influenced in a particular direction. This increases the effectiveness of manipulation exponentially. “Within such an environment, these actors seek to use the infrastructure of digital platforms themselves, rather than resorting to conventional propaganda methods, to promote foreign values, undermine national stability, and divide our society from within. “Monitoring has also established that, despite the scale of malicious activities directed against Azerbaijan from certain centers, our Victorious People have demonstrated a resolute stance, refused to succumb to provocations, unequivocally supported the measures taken by the state, and continue to provide the necessary assistance in exposing divisive content and the individuals behind it. “We reiterate that the parliament's Commission on Foreign Interference and Hybrid Threats, the relevant parliamentary committees and structural divisions of the parliamentary administration, together with the relevant state institutions, are successfully countering these malicious hybrid attacks against our state and will continue to respond decisively to any future attempt. “Our commission also expresses its profound gratitude to citizens of friendly and neighboring countries who have condemned these anti-Azerbaijani activities and demonstrated a fair and principled position.” Tags: Azerbaijan Parliament war

https://asiaplus.news/en/2026/10/15/parl.body: Share Mehrofarin Najibi , asia+ Categories Communication Law-order Security Society Tajikistan Format News Published 15.10.2026 17:07 Tajikistan’s lower house of parliament, the Majlisi Namoyandagon, has ratified the UN Convention against Cybercrime, paving the way for greater international cooperation in cybercrime investigations and the exchange of electronic evidence. Lawmakers approved the convention on October 1. Its text was later published by Sadoi Mardum , the parliament’s official newspaper. The document, commonly known as the Hanoi Convention, establishes a framework for international cooperation in combating crimes committed using information and communication technologies and exchanging electronic evidence related to serious crimes. What does the convention provide? MP Dilnoza Ahmadzoda said the UN General Assembly adopted the convention on December 24, 2024. It consists of nine chapters and 68 articles, along with an annex. According to Ahmadzoda, its main objective is to establish a common international framework for preventing and combating cybercrime. The convention provides for stronger cooperation between law enforcement agencies, the exchange of information and electronic evidence, the seizure of criminal assets and the recovery of proceeds from crime. It is also intended to make cybercrime investigations more effective. Ahmadzoda highlighted its relevance to internet fraud, unauthorized access to information systems, digital data theft, transnational crime and the protection of children online. Why is international cooperation necessary? First Deputy Prosecutor-General Umed Karimzoda told lawmakers that cybercrime frequently crosses national borders, while evidence and traces of criminal activity may be stored in different countries. “Effective combat against cybercrime cannot be limited to the capabilities of a single state,” he said. Karimzoda also stressed the growing importance of timely information exchange, mutual legal assistance and access to electronic evidence across jurisdictions. He noted that the rapid development of information and communication technologies and the digitalization of the economy have created new opportunities for crime, including online fraud and the illegal use of digital data. How did Tajikistan join the convention? Tajikistan signed the convention at the United Nations headquarters in New York on March 17, 2026. President Emomali Rahmon subsequently submitted it to the Majlisi Namoyandagon for ratification. Ahmadzoda said the document does not contradict Tajikistan’s Constitution, laws or other regulatory legal acts. Lawmakers approved the ratification resolution without questions or debate. What cybercrime schemes have been reported in Tajikistan? Cybercrime, including the theft of money from electronic wallets, has been reported in Tajikistan for several years. In one scheme, fraudsters call citizens under the pretext of switching to a 5G network and steal money from their bank cards and digital wallets. In other cases, attackers have used messages such as “Is this you in the photo?” on Telegram and WhatsApp to trick users into compromising their phones and gaining access to their digital wallets. The convention is intended to strengthen the international cooperation needed to investigate such crimes when perpetrators, victims and electronic evidence are located in different countries. "Voting began today at Israeli embassies, consulates and diplomatic missions abroad ahead of the parliamentary elections to be held in Israel on October 27," the statement said. Under Israeli law, early voting at diplomatic missions abroad is open to Israeli citizens who are on long-term official assignments in the respective countries, as well as their family members. The Foreign Ministry noted that Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who is visiting Baku, observed the voting process at the Israeli Embassy in Azerbaijan. It should be noted that the elections for the 26th Knesset are scheduled for Tuesday, October 27. Their outcome will determine the composition of the governing coalition and opposition, the next prime minister and the future of Israel’s 38th government. The eyes of the whole world are focused on the Karabakh region these days. Thank you very much for receiving us. - Thank you. - Mr. President, of course, we will start our conversation with the situation in the region. Yesterday Armenia fired on civilians yet again. In Tartar, a cemetery was fired on and three of our Azerbaijani brothers became martyrs. What is your assessment of this attack? - This is yet another manifestation of Armenian fascism. Usually, whenever they are defeated on the battlefield, they fire on civilians. We saw this during the first Karabakh war. It was our loathsome neighbors who committed the Khojaly genocide. This time, seeing their helplessness in front of the Azerbaijani army on the battlefield and their inability to resist us in the occupied lands, they started targeting civilians again. Our citizens died as a result of this dastardly attack, both in Ganja and at the cemetery in Tartar yesterday... This is a place where people go for funerals, it is considered sacred to any person. But apparently there is nothing "sacred" for our loathsome neighbors. This is a crime against humanity, which once again demonstrates the predatory nature of Armenia. It also shows that such dastardly attacks cannot force us to deviate from our path, they cannot break the will of the Azerbaijani people. We will continue to restore our territorial integrity. - Of course, Azerbaijan acts very carefully and accurately in the issue of civilians. Until today, not a single civilian has been hurt among the Armenians. However, up to now 46 of our Azerbaijani brothers have become martyrs. Why does the West remain tight-lipped over these massacres? - Unfortunately, civilian casualties are continuing, there are already 47. A total of 222 civilians have been injured, about 2,000 houses have been either completely destroyed or seriously damaged. I have already said that we will avenge these people on the battlefield. We have never opened and are still not opening fire on civilians despite the fact that there have been attacks on Ganja and Tartar. Today, from 6 to 8 am – it is 9:10 now – more than 220 shells fell on Tartar, Aghdam, Goranboy and other districts. So these heinous attacks continue. Their main goal is to kill civilians, sow panic and fear among the population of Azerbaijan, stop us and achieve their dirty intentions. But they are seeing that this does not work out, and no matter how many shells fall, the citizens of Azerbaijan proudly live on their land and endure all these difficulties. They are united around one goal – to return Karabakh, to raise the flag of Azerbaijan in all the occupied lands and to restore our territorial integrity. As for your second question why the West is silent, we saw this during the first Karabakh war too. Armenia unleashed aggression against us, occupied our lands, committed genocide against our people, but sanctions were applied against Azerbaijan. At that time, in 1992 and 1993, the Western media formed such a perception that Azerbaijan was an occupier and aggressor, while Armenia was a victim of aggression. We are seeing this even today on a smaller scale, because it is no longer possible to deny and hide the truth. - Mr. President, at that time, in 1993, in particular, in November, a ceasefire was also announced. And it was also violated by Armenia, which massacred people. Today Armenia wants a ceasefire again. What is the purpose of the ceasefire – to stop the advance of the Azerbaijani army? - You know, this is their tactic. Armenia requested a ceasefire. Convinced that they could no longer defend the occupied lands on the battlefield, to hold on to them, they requested a ceasefire. We also received such an appeal – you know that Russia has undertaken this mission – and said that a ceasefire could be declared for humanitarian purposes, for the exchange of bodies and prisoners. However, at the same time, the Moscow statement indicated that it was necessary to resume negotiations on the substance of the issue. In addition, the format of the negotiations should remain unchanged. But apparently they wanted to take advantage of the ceasefire. Less than a day later this dastardly attack on Ganja was carried out. After that, they began to strike at our other cities and, in fact, grossly violated the ceasefire. So this is their tactic. Obviously, they needed a ceasefire in order to gather strength, take mobilization measures and launch new attacks on us, because after this ceasefire, they tried to occupy the settlement of Hadrut again and attacked it three times. And they were defeated all three times. Their intention is to return the lands they lost that do not belong to them and to continue their aggressive policy. - By the way, false propaganda is currently being conducted. They claim that Hadrut is still with them, they cannot accept it. - Yes, they are still engaged in this false propaganda. The Azerbaijani flag has been flying in Hadrut for several days now. The vast majority of the hills adjacent to Hadrut are under our control. If Hadrut had not been taken, it would have been impossible to take the villages of Khojavand district. We moved there only from the Hadrut direction. - Mr. President, since the announcement of the humanitarian ceasefire, transport planes have been constantly delivering missiles from Russia, in particular, to the Yerevan airport. This, in essence, is a crime. In particular, you talked about the closure of borders with Iranian President Rouhani and about the delivery of missiles with Russia. These weapons are provided free of charge. What would you like to say to Iran and Russia in this regard? - We do not have any information about the shipment of weapons from Iran to Armenia. On the contrary, I can say that Iran and Georgia have closed their airspace and land roads for the transportation of weapons to Armenia. In this regard, we would like to reiterate our gratitude to the Governments of Iran and Georgia. According to our information, weapons are being smuggled across Georgian territory by commercial and cargo planes. Armenia has recently purchased one plane. According to our information, it bought it for $30-40 million. It was purchased by wealthy Armenian businessmen living in Russia – Karapetyan, Abrahamyan and others. They are sending Armenians living in Russia to fight against us as mercenaries. Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani thanked the Azerbaijani President for the reception and praised the excellent organization of the CICA Summit, noting that Azerbaijan had extensive experience in successfully hosting international events. The Amir also said that the development he had witnessed in Baku had made a deep impression on him. The President of Azerbaijan and the Amir of Qatar welcomed the development of relations between the two countries, exchanged views on prospects for cooperation, and discussed the activities of the intergovernmental commission. Ilham Aliyev asked Wang Yi to convey his warm greetings and best wishes to President Xi Jinping, and expressed gratitude to President Xi Jinping for sending a special representative to attend the CICA Summit in Azerbaijan. Ilham Aliyev noted that China and Azerbaijan enjoy deep political mutual trust and mutually beneficial economic cooperation, and the Azerbaijan-China comprehensive strategic partnership is flourishing. The consensus he reached with President Xi Jinping during his visit to China last year has been effectively implemented, ushering the bilateral relations into a new stage. Azerbaijan appreciates China’s long-standing strong support for Azerbaijan’s economic and social development and the safeguarding of its national interests. It regards China as a leading force in the rise of the Global South, and believes Chinese modernization has set an example for developing countries including Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan is one of the first countries to support and participate in the Belt and Road Initiative. A series of cooperation projects between the two countries have yielded fruitful results. Azerbaijan is ready to strengthen strategic alignment with China and continue to expand cooperation in energy, connectivity and other fields. Azerbaijan welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in the country. The two countries should make good use of the mutual visa exemption to further promote their people‐to‐people exchanges. Azerbaijan firmly adheres to the one‐China principle, fully supports the series of global initiatives put forward by President Xi Jinping, appreciates China’s consistent commitment to upholding international fairness and justice and multilateralism, and is ready to strengthen coordination and cooperation with China in international and regional affairs. China appreciates Azerbaijan’s long-standing strong support on issues concerning China’s core interests, and supports Azerbaijan in safeguarding its independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. China’s development represents the increasing force of the Global South and the growing strength of developing countries. China is ready to maintain close coordination and cooperation with Azerbaijan to jointly safeguard the common interests of Global South countries. China supports Azerbaijan in playing an important role in multilateral platforms such as CICA and in international affairs, and making greater contributions to peace and stability of the region and the world. During the visit, Wang Yi also held talks with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov.

https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-and-the-t.body: Features Russia And The Taliban Are Drawing Closer. What's In It For Both Sides? By Daud Khattak October 15, 2026 11:27 CET Russia And The Taliban Are Drawing Closer. What's In It For Both Sides? Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Taliban security and defense forces are looking to bolster their arsenal with Russian military hardware. Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev arrived in Islamabad this week for the first official visit by the country’s top domestic affairs official, highlighting growing concerns in Moscow about regional security on its southern flank. Kolokoltsev's visit comes days after a meeting of the Moscow Format Consultations on Afghanistan -- which also includes Russia, China, India, and Iran -- where Pakistani and Taliban representatives clashed over allegations of their countries’ support for militants who could threaten stability well beyond their borders. Official statements from Islamabad and Moscow have emphasized the strengthening of mutual ties, but analysts said Kolokoltsev’s four-day visit is more about Russia’s fears about the regional presence of Islamic State Khorasan Province (IS-K), known for high-profile assaults including the 2021 Kabul airport bombing, the 2024 Kerman bombings in Iran, and the 2024 Crocus City Hall attack in Russia. Challenging Islamic State While Moscow has been growing diplomatic ties with Kabul in hopes of reining in IS-K, an affiliate of the Islamic State extremist group, Taliban authorities have their eyes fixed on Russian military hardware, including drones, to counterbalance their erstwhile ally, Pakistan. Moscow's increasingly accommodating stance toward the Taliban has sparked widespread international criticism of the group's sweeping restrictions on women's rights and its harsh treatment of political opponents. SEE ALSO: Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation' “The warming ties between Moscow and Kabul are not part of a new alliance, but a layered regional realignment,” said Omar Samad, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who also served as Afghanistan's ambassador to Canada and France under the previous administration. Russia “gets a low-cost Afghan buffer on Central Asia’s vulnerable flank,” Samad told RFE/RL. “Such cooperation could help Moscow contain threats from Islamic State-Khorasan, Islamic State's regional affiliate and an ideological rival of the Taliban.” Russia's concern about IS-K was highlighted in May by Aleksandr Bortnikov, head of the country’s Federal Security Service (FSB), who warned that the group was recruiting citizens of Central Asian countries and migrant workers inside Russia. In July 2025, Russia became the first country to formally recognize the Taliban government, and it remains the only one to have done so. Unlike in the 1990s, when Russia supplied arms and provided assistance to forces fighting the Taliban, Moscow has come to accept the militant Islamists as a political reality, seeking to protect its security interests in Central Asia, particularly along Afghanistan's northern borders. Cooperation Agreement In May, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu and Taliban Defense Minister Mohammad Yaqoob signed a military-technical cooperation agreement in Moscow. The agreement's full terms have not been made public, although Yaqoob said it focused on repairing and maintaining Russian-made military equipment already in Afghanistan. In a study published in the Journal of Asian Security and International Affairs in 2025, researchers Tatiana Belousova and Raghav Sharma argued that Moscow's warming relations with the Taliban reflected a pragmatic reassessment of Russia's security interests, particularly its concerns about the threat posed by IS-K. SEE ALSO: Afghan Women Build Businesses As Taliban Restrictions Shrink Their Options But while counterterrorism is a key Russian priority, the Taliban is seeking military assistance to strengthen its defenses, particularly against Pakistani air strikes. After returning from Moscow in late May, Yaqoob said Pakistan would soon no longer dare attack Afghan territory, although he also stressed that the agreement with Russia was not a mutual-defense pact. Pakistan and Taliban forces have repeatedly clashed along their shared border, with tensions escalating after Pakistani air strikes on Kabul and other Afghan locations in October 2025. Pakistan had previously carried out strikes inside Afghanistan, including in March and December 2024. Further strikes and retaliatory attacks followed in 2026. Pakistan, which supported the Afghan Taliban for decades, accuses Kabul of sheltering the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, an Islamist militant group that has carried out deadly attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians. The Afghan Taliban denies harboring the group. SEE ALSO: Families Torn Apart, Trade At A Standstill: One Year Of The Afghan-Pakistan Border Closure For Moscow, however, counterterrorism remains central to its engagement with Kabul, with recent reports of more direct Russian assistance to Taliban forces. In June, citing two sources within the Taliban's Defense Ministry, Afghanistan International claimed that Russia was helping finance, train, and equip a new 8,000-member Taliban special forces unit. The unit, known as the Hibati Unit, would reportedly conduct operations against IS-K and help secure Afghanistan's border with Pakistan. “Moscow publicly articulates an acute terrorist threat emanating from Afghan soil while simultaneously deepening ties with the Taliban,” geopolitical analyst Eldaniz Gusseinov wrote in The Diplomat. “That is the dual character of the Russian strategy. The threat narrative reinforces a self-assigned security role across Central Asia; the partnership with Kabul provides the instrument for that role.” The Taliban is also said to have stepped up drone surveillance in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhshan, where armed opposition groups remain active. Russia has not indicated that it is supplying drone technology to the Taliban or assisting in its development. However, Afghanistan International reported on October 1, citing former senior Afghan officials, that the Taliban was seeking to acquire drones and other military equipment from Belarus, a close Russian ally, allegedly with India's financial assistance and Moscow's approval. The claims have not been independently verified. Samad said Russia's growing cooperation with the Taliban had caused unease in Pakistan, although Iran and China shared Moscow's interest in limiting Western military influence in Afghanistan and the wider region. For the Taliban, the benefits are both diplomatic and military, though the latter remains limited in scope. “The Taliban gets formal recognition, support for its counterterrorism and anti-narcotics efforts, and inexpensive help keeping Soviet-era armor and helicopters serviceable, a hedge against Pakistani strikes, not a new arsenal as of yet,” Samad said. https://www.rferl.org/a/eu-limits-russia.body: News EU Working On Multiple Fronts To Limit Russians From Entering Bloc By Rikard Jozwiak October 14, 2026 15:11 CET EU Working On Multiple Fronts To Limit Russians From Entering Bloc Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google A border guard checks a driver's papers at a crossing between Russia and Finland. (file photo) BRUSSELS -- The European Union is working on multiple fronts to limit the number of Russian citizens that can enter the bloc, including the nuclear option of a total ban on all non-essential travel into the club’s Schengen zone. This comes as Brussels and several EU member states have flagged that individuals using either Russian diplomatic cover or traveling on tourism visas have played key roles in various types of hybrid attacks in the bloc. Most recently, German authorities revealed that the main suspect of the drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which caused major traffic disruptions, was a Belarusian-Russian citizen who entered the EU using an Italian-issued Schengen tourist visa. In a leaked EU presidency policy paper on various Russian visa options, seen by RFE/RL, it is noted that the “only long-term and effective solution would appear to be the possibility to adopt visa restrictive measures, which would ban non-essential travel for one nationality of applicants.” The document notes that changes to the EU visa code would be necessary for such a move and that “these visa measures would be applied in a uniform way as EU law”. A change to the visa code would be made via qualified majority, constituting 55 percent of all member states, representing 65 percent of the total EU population. A bigger overhaul of the EU visa code could come later in the year but several EU member states, notably in southern Europe, are still reluctant to completely shut down various avenues of people-to-people contact with Russian citizens. SEE ALSO: Wider Europe Briefing: What To Expect At The EU's October Summit Shortly after the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU fully suspended the EU-Russia visa facilitation agreement that allowed for cheaper visas, multiple-entry visas and simpler procedures to obtain them. Brussels also issued guidelines to EU member states on how to deal with Russian visa applications, prioritizing so-called “essential travel” requests such as applicants going for humanitarian reasons, including civil society representatives, political dissidents and independent journalists or family reunification. Patchwork Approach These guidelines are nonbinding, giving each EU member state wide discretion on how they would treat Russian visa applications. And the result has created a European patchwork of approaches to Russian visa requests. While many countries on the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Russia, imposed very strict rules by hardly allowing any Russian nationals to enter, southern member states, keen on summer visitors, were more generous in issuing Schengen tourist visas for Russian citizens. In 2025, a record since the full-scale invasion was reached, with 477,878 visas being issued to Russian nationals for tourism purposes. The vast majority of those were authorized by Greece, Italy, France, and Spain. SEE ALSO: Montenegro To Expel Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Rybar Until a potential decision on a full entry ban could be taken, the EU is working in parallel on three separate tracks on how to reduce the number of Russian visitors -- banning ex-combatants in Ukraine, reducing Russian diplomatic movement and so-called “limited territorial validity (LTV)” visas, which only allows you to stay in the country that issued the visa while prohibiting the holder from travelling to other Schengen zone countries. The presidency paper notes that “LTV visas are presented as an interim measure, pending the future implementation of a full ban on travel for non-essential purposes.” Germany has argued for this approach and the paper notes that the rationale behind the push is to let the countries that still issue non-essential visas to Russian to “assume full responsibility for doing so, in a context where other Member States adopt a much stricter approach.” But the paper also points out the limits with this move, noting that “this runs against one of the basic principles on which the Schengen area is based, i.e. mutual trust. It amounts to a re-nationalization of short-stay visa policy”. Limited Effect The very fact that there hardly are any internal EU border controls also make an LTV visa have limited effect with the document stating that “an LTV visa issued to a Russian national with malevolent intent does not seem to offer sufficient security guarantees against further movements inside the Schengen Area.” Regarding ex-combatants travelling on tourist visas, movement is expected soon. Various European consulates in Russia will most likely be required to check military service documents as part of the visa issuance routine. There are still some issues, however, such as the fact that many of the consulate staff are Russian citizens and that Moscow, according to European diplomats familiar with the matter, has threatened them with legal action if they ask about such documentation. In a separate diplomatic note, seen by RFE/RL, the case for restricting the movement of Russian diplomats and consular staff within the EU is also being explored. The common practice right now stipulates that Russian diplomatic personnel in the EU are only required to notify authorities when traveling to another member state, but there is now a push to introduce a requirement to obtain prior authorization from the country they intend to visit. Another idea gaining traction in Brussels is to limit how long Russian diplomats and officials can remain in their host countries as European counterintelligence services are keen to curb long-established spy networks, in which diplomats stationed in one place for extended periods often play a key role. EU Working On Multiple Fronts To Limit Russians From Entering Bloc Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print Rikard Jozwiak Rikard Jozwiak is the Europe editor for RFE/RL in Prague, focusing on coverage of the European Union and NATO. He previously worked as RFE/RL’s Brussels correspondent, covering numerous international summits, European elections, and international court rulings. He has reported from most European capitals, as well as Central Asia. This item is part of News Russia Europe

https://www.rferl.org/a/azerbaijan-hijab.body: Azerbaijan Schools In Azerbaijan Turn Away Girls Wearing Hijabs As Debate Over Religious Freedom Intensifies By RFE/RL's Azerbaijani Service October 14, 2026 15:50 CET Schools In Azerbaijan Turn Away Girls Wearing Hijabs As Debate Over Religious Freedom Intensifies Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Parents in Baku and elsewhere say school administrations have told girls to remove their head scarves or barred them from classes. (file photo) Parents and students in Azerbaijan are protesting Azerbaijan's new rules on school uniforms following reports that schools were turning away girls wearing hijabs as the dispute over religious freedom and secular education escalated in the Muslim-majority country. The amendment, approved by the Cabinet of Ministers on September 21, prohibits clothing deemed as violating the requirements for school uniforms or conflicting with secular education principles. The hijab is not explicitly mentioned, leaving schools to interpret how the rules apply. Parents in Baku and elsewhere say school administrations have told girls to remove their head scarves or barred them from classes. Some students have boycotted lessons. The Interior Ministry said on October 12 that 37 people had been detained for refusing to comply with the new rules and attempting to disrupt public order. Embed share Girls In Hijabs Turned Away From Azerbaijani Schools Amid Protests Over Dress Code by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:45 0:00 The dispute has escalated an already heated debate in Azerbaijan over whether restricting religious dress in schools protects children from pressure or infringes on their rights. "Children are still in the formation stage. Their worldview, choices, and decisions are often determined by the influence of the family and environment," said Elnara Akimova, a lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), who supported the tightened rules. She told RFE/RL that the amendments were intended to provide a neutral educational environment. But critics argue that the vague application of the rules creates an unnecessary barrier to a child's right to an education. Gulmira Aslanova, a parent in Baku, told RFE/RL that the administration of School No. 172 in the capital's Narimanov district told her to send her daughter to school without a head scarf. She said the restrictions conflicted with constitutional guarantees of religious freedom and education. SEE ALSO: Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen "In our country, secondary education is compulsory, and every student must study at school," Aslanova said, adding that those who prevent children from studying should be held accountable. Parents in the southern town of Jalilabad made similar complaints. Sociologist Sanubar Heydarova said children should continue attending school while the legal dispute is resolved. She argued that their right to education should not come at the expense of their cultural identity. Recurring Dispute The controversy echoes a 2010 dispute over school uniforms that did not accommodate the hijab. Hundreds protested in Baku that December, and police broke up subsequent rallies. The controversy continued into 2011. Azerbaijan's constitution defines the country as secular while also safeguarding religious freedom. But the government of the oil-rich nation of some 10.5 million maintains tight control over religious activity. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent federal commission, recommended in its 2026 annual report that Azerbaijan remain on the State Department's Special Watch List for "severe violations of religious freedom." SEE ALSO: Tajikistan Expands Crackdown On Head Scarves, Beards In New Push For 'National Culture' USCIRF head Vicky Hartzler argued the country should instead be designated a Country of Particular Concern. "Azerbaijan outwardly claims to support religious freedom, yet inwardly does the opposite," Hartzler wrote. She cited government control over religious activity, including the appointment of imams, approval of religious materials, requirements on the registration of churches, and state involvement in writing sermons for Muslim services. Regional Debate Over Religious Dress The dispute has drawn condemnation in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protests were held outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul, while an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said it ⁠was "unacceptable" to deny the right to education for students wearing a hijab. "We expect Azerbaijan to reverse this mistake as soon as possible," the adviser, Oktay Saral, wrote on X. Azerbaijan's ruling party condemned Saral's comments as "irresponsible" and warned they risked ⁠harming relations between the close allies. On social media, some recalled Turkey's own restrictions on head scarves at universities and in public institutions that were gradually lifted between 2010 and 2017. SEE ALSO: Where Did Iran's Hijab Police Go? The hijab has been a point of contention in the region in recent years. In Iran, a historic protest movement Women, Life, Freedom erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old student, in police custody after being arrested for an allegedly "improper hijab." The movement rapidly transformed from a grievance over state-mandated Islamic dress codes into the most significant challenge to the Islamic republic since the 1979 revolution, fundamentally changing the dynamic between the Iranian public and the ruling regime. Meanwhile in Central Asia, staunchly secular governments have banned or restricted head scarves in schools and workplaces, prompting criticism from Muslim citizens and rights defenders. Officials in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan have been condemned for organizing raids on the streets that targeted women wearing hijabs. https://ashgabat.osce.org/news/centre-as.body: News News Item OSCE lecture course introduces Turkmenistan’s law students to principles of humanitarian law in conflict and post-conflict situations Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Centre in Ashgabat Fields of work: Human rights , Education Key principles of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in the context of conflict and post-conflict situations were the focus of an OSCE-organized lecture course held in Ashgabat from 12 to 14 October 2026. The three-day course took place at the International University for Humanities and Development (IUHD) and brought together 50 law students and faculty members from the IUHD, the Institute of International Relations (IIR) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Turkmenistan, and the Institute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. International experts from Austria shared their expertise in international human rights law, international humanitarian law, international criminal law, and international refugee and migration law, highlighting the distinctive characteristics of these legal frameworks and their relation with national legislation. “The knowledge you have gained during this training course will be useful for your future professional careers and will help you better understand the links between international legal norms, OSCE commitments and their practical application,” said William Leaf, Head of the OSCE Centre in Ashgabat. The lecture course also addressed the protection of women, children and other vulnerable groups; the treatment of detainees and prisoners of war; and the investigation of alleged cases of torture in accordance with international human rights law and international humanitarian law. Students also learned about international accountability mechanisms and approaches to addressing the consequences of human rights violations. https://odihr.osce.org/news/odihr/668703.body: News News Item ODIHR event focuses on supporting Roma rights defenders in Ukraine Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Fields of work: Human rights , Roma and Sinti , Tolerance and non-discrimination Roma rights activists discussed how to strengthen their work to combat discrimination and protect human rights during the war in Ukraine at an event organized by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) in Warsaw. Roma and pro-Roma human rights defenders help combat discrimination and seek remedies for human rights violations affecting Roma. The war following the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine has added to the existing risks, making sustained support for their safety and security essential. “Building and enhancing the capacity of Roma civil society has been a crucial pillar of ODIHR’s intervention in Ukraine. It is of paramount importance to redouble our efforts to provide protection, opportunities and resources for them,” said ODIHR First Deputy Director Tea Jaliashvili. Participants shared their experiences of advocating for the protection and promotion of Roma rights during the war. They discussed how state and non-state stakeholders can better respond to activists’ needs, and how capacity development can support efforts to tackle discrimination and pursue justice. “Legal and policy guarantees alone do not ensure the access of Roma women to healthcare services. A lasting change requires institutional accountability, effective protection against discrimination, and meaningful participation of Roma women in shaping these services intended to meet their needs. The safety of Roma human rights defenders, particularly women, is integral to this work. Documenting violations and advocating for our communities must not subject us to threats, intimidation or reprisals,” said Anna Burdeina, a Roma human rights defender from Ukraine. ODIHR’s support combines training, mentoring and follow-up assistance in human rights monitoring, advocacy, gender empowerment, digital safety and security, and well-being. The three activists speaking at the event are taking part in an ODIHR advocacy programme that has been running since December 2025. The discussion took place at an ODIHR side event during the 2026 Warsaw Human Dimension Conference , as part of the Programme on Support for and Engagement in Ukraine. https://bih.osce.org/news/mission-bosnia.body: News News Item The OSCE Mission and University of Sarajevo join forces to turn human rights education into practice Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina SARAJEVO, 14 October 2026 – University of Sarajevo students will have the opportunity to learn directly from experts how to address real-life human rights challenges through a new partnership between the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Faculty of Political Sciences. Formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding signed today, the partnership will introduce a semester-long programme for third-year students, scheduled to begin in early 2027. The programme is envisaged to be accredited for 10 ECTS credits and will combine classroom learning with practical experience and insights from professionals working in the field. “Protecting human rights requires more than strong legal frameworks. It also requires professionals who understand how to apply these standards in practice. Through this partnership, we aim to connect academic knowledge with real-life challenges, equip students with practical skills, and contribute to stronger human rights protection in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” said Rick Holtzapple, Head of the OSCE Mission to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sead Turčalo, Dean of the Faculty of Political Sciences, University of Sarajevo, emphasized that the signing of the Memorandum represents a strategic step in its continued efforts to enhance the quality of education. “Through interactive engagement with experts, work on real-life case studies and mentoring support, our students will acquire practical skills essential for their future professional careers. Our vision at the Faculty of Political Sciences is to educate young people who not only understand contemporary societal challenges but are also equipped with the practical skills needed to address them. This strong partnership with the OSCE Mission enables us to turn that vision into reality.” The partnership will also open opportunities for students from other faculties and disciplines, including Political Science, Sociology, and Journalism and Communications, through expert lectures, workshops, case studies and joint research. The first year of the Memorandum’s implementation will focus on combating violence against women and domestic violence. Through this programme, students will have the opportunity to familiarize themselves with recent legislative developments and gain practical insight into the application of legal provisions and protective measures in this field. By connecting students with practitioners, the initiative aims to prepare future professionals to better recognize, prevent and respond to human rights violations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

https://montenegro.osce.org/news/mission.body: News News Item OSCE Mission to Montenegro strengthens police capacity for ethical interviewing and evidence recording Issued on: 15 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Policing Ethical police interviews and reliable evidence recording are help protect victims’ and witnesses’ rights, ensure fair proceedings, and build public trust in law enforcement. Following request from a broad range of stakeholders, from journalists to the Police Directorate, the OSCE Mission to Montenegro organized a training session in Podgorica on 14 and 15 October on ethical interviewing and the proper use of recording equipment. By the end of the year, the Mission will also provide recording equipment to security departments in Berane, Bijelo Polje, Podgorica and Rožaje. Sixteen police officers took part in the training, guided by a psychologist and a clinical psychologist. They explored techniques for children and adults, the effects of trauma on memory, and ways to safeguard victims’ and witnesses’ rights. Opening the workshop, the Head of the OSCE Mission to Montenegro, Ambassador Jan Haukaas, stated that this training reflected a shared commitment to fair, profession, and lawful police interviews. “The interview is one of the most important tools available to the police. It is often the first point of direct interaction between a person and the police, whether that person is a victim, witness, suspect, journalist or another individual providing information. How this interaction is conducted affects both the reliability of the information obtained and whether the individual feels respected, safe, and able to provide an accurate account” said Ambassador Haukaas. He further stated that “Clear, impartial questioning and careful listening are essential to avoiding misunderstandings, protecting individual rights and ensuring the integrity of investigations.” Assistant Director of Police for the General Jurisdiction Police Sector, Haris Đurđević, noted that the provision and installation of recording equipment was among the requirements under the standards of the Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) that Montenegro is obliged to implement, particularly to protect human rights and vulnerable groups. “This training and the equipment that will be provided by the OSCE Mission represent significant support for the work of the Police Directorate and, at the same time, a safeguard for police officers facing unfounded allegations of abuse and torture,” said Đurđević. The two-day training addressed both the legal and psychological aspects of interviewing, with particular emphasis on engaging with vulnerable groups. It aimed not only to strengthen officers’ practical interviewing skills but also to reinforce their responsibility to uphold professional and legal standards. Properly conducted and recorded interviews contribute to the reliability of evidence, the fairness of criminal proceedings and, ultimately, public trust in the police. The training aimed to strengthen officers’ practical skills and reinforce professional standards, helping to promote reliable evidence, fair proceedings, and greater public confidence in the police. https://odihr.osce.org/news/odihr/668664.body: News News Item New ODIHR handbook brings Roma and Sinti electoral participation into focus at Warsaw conference Issued on: 14 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights Fields of work: Elections , Roma and Sinti , Tolerance and non-discrimination Ensuring that Roma and Sinti can participate meaningfully in elections requires sustained efforts to identify and remove the barriers they continue to face as voters, candidates and participants in public and political life. This was the message from participants at a Warsaw Human Dimension Conference side event organized by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR). “These challenges remind us that legal guarantees alone are not sufficient. Full and effective participation also requires that we understand how electoral processes operate in practice, identify where barriers exist, and work systematically towards removing them,” said ODIHR First Deputy Director Tea Jaliashvili. The event marked the launch of ODIHR’s new Handbook on Observing and Promoting the Participation of Roma and Sinti in Electoral Processes , developed jointly by ODIHR’s Election Department and Contact Point for Roma and Sinti Issues. Drawing on ODIHR’s longstanding election observation methodology and its work to promote the participation of Roma and Sinti in public and political life, the handbook provides practical guidance on assessing participation throughout the electoral cycle and identifying obstacles that may prevent Roma and Sinti from exercising their electoral rights on an equal basis. Roma and Sinti continue to face a range of barriers to meaningful electoral participation. These can include discrimination and anti-Roma rhetoric, difficulties registering to vote and obtaining identification documents, pressure and vote-buying, limited access to voter information, and under-representation among candidates and elected representatives. Roma and Sinti women and young people may face additional and intersecting barriers to taking part in political and public life. “Meaningful participation is not only about being able to cast a vote. Roma and Sinti need to have a real voice in political life, to stand as candidates, influence decisions and participate on an equal footing. We need to understand the barriers communities experience and ensure that their perspectives are reflected in how electoral processes are designed, assessed and improved,” said Lucie Fuková, Roma activist and former Government Commissioner for Roma Minority Affairs of the Czech Republic. Intended for election observers, public authorities, Roma and Sinti civil society organizations, and other stakeholders, the handbook looks beyond election day to participation throughout the electoral cycle, covering the legal framework, voter and candidate registration, election administration, election campaigns, the media, voting and post-election follow-up. Participants discussed how to put the handbook’s guidance into practice through election observation, civil society monitoring, voter education, advocacy and follow-up to electoral recommendations. They also explored how institutions, civil society and other stakeholders can work together to ensure that the experiences and concerns of Roma and Sinti are systematically reflected in efforts to make electoral processes more inclusive. https://cpj.org/2026/10/taliban-suspends.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New York, October 14, 2026—The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Taliban authorities to immediately and unconditionally restore the FM radio transmissions of British public broadcaster BBC across Afghanistan, end the devastating crackdown on independent media, and cease restricting Afghan’s access to independent news and information. On October 13, the Taliban confirmed that they had suspended BBC World Service programming from FM radio transmitters across Afghanistan, affecting the broadcaster’s Dari, Pashto, and English-language services, according to the BBC and news reports . BBC said it continues to provide news and programming for Afghan audiences in the three languages through shortwave and medium-wave radio, satellite, and online services. “By forcing BBC off Afghanistan’s FM broadcasts, the Taliban are further shrinking an already devastated space for independent journalism in the country,” said Waliullah Rahmani, CPJ’s Afghanistan and Pakistan representative. “The Taliban must immediately reverse the suspension, explain the legal basis for their action, and end their systematic obstruction of Afghans’ access to independent information.” Khabib Ghufran, spokesperson for the Taliban-controlled Ministry of Information and Culture, said the BBC’s activities had been suspended “for the time being” because of what he described as “repeated violations,” without elaborating . London-based broadcaster Afghanistan International reported, citing unnamed sources, that the Taliban’s dissatisfaction with a recent BBC documentary may have contributed to the decision. In March 2022, Taliban authorities ordered local television stations to stop carrying local-language programming from international broadcasters, including the BBC, the U.S. Congress-funded Voice of America, and German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle. The order removed BBC television bulletins in Pashto, Persian, and Uzbek from Afghan partner stations. In December 2022, authorities also removed Voice of America and U.S. Congress-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty from Afghanistan’s AM and FM networks, citing unspecified complaints about their programming. The Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture did not respond to CPJ’s email seeking comment. https://cpj.org/2026/10/cpj-partners-cal.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email The Committee to Protect Journalists joined Albanian and international partner organizations in an open letter calling on Albanian authorities to investigate repeated violence and obstruction affecting journalists covering protests, and ensure accountability. The letter came after serious incidents in the capital Tirana on October 13, when several journalists reported being physically assaulted or obstructed by police officers during protests over education and social issues. Three media workers required hospital treatment. This was not an isolated incident. On October 8, journalists covering a protest outside parliament were obstructed by police despite being identifiable as members of the media, and some were pepper-sprayed. In September , Citizens.al journalist Vjolanda Peca was briefly detained while reporting on a protest. The signatories to the letter called on police, oversight bodies, prosecutors, and government institutions to investigate the incidents, preserve relevant evidence, implement existing journalist safety guidelines, and ensure that journalists can report safely and without obstruction at public assemblies. The letter urged the European Union, Council of Europe, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) to raise the groups’ concerns with Albanian authorities. It also stressed that effective protection of journalists and implementation of fundamental rights and safeguards are part of Albania’s commitments as part of the process of European Union accession. https://cpj.org/2026/10/turkish-authorit.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, October 14, 2026—Turkish authorities must immediately return control of Halk TV, one of the few remaining media voices critical of the government, to its staff and cease their relentless efforts to stifle the free flow of information in the country, the Committee to Protect Journalists said Wednesday. Police officers raided Halk TV’s headquarters in Istanbul Wednesday morning , stopping live broadcasts and preventing staff from entering the building, although some posted on X that they were later allowed in. Halk TV said on X that authorities assigned a trustee, or administrator, to take over the outlet, while news reports said the raid was linked to a criminal investigation into owner Cafer Mahiroğlu , whose other assets were seized as well. Mahiroğlu, who lives abroad, said in a video message on X that seven of his relatives in Turkey were in police custody, and that the accusations against him were false. “Seizing Halk TV strikes at the heart of press freedom in Turkey where the vast majority of news outlets are pro-government. Halk TV is one of the very few remaining broadcasters that criticize the government and this action is a devastating blow to the Turkish people’s right to freedom of information and expression,” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “Control of Halk TV must immediately be returned to its staff and this deeply alarming and damaging crackdown on journalism must end.” Turkey is witnessing an intense and sustained crackdown on independent and pro-opposition media, with dozens of journalists arrested or detained so far this year. Turkish authorities have also blocked access to thousands of social media accounts belonging to journalists and rights defenders. In October last year, authorities also seized the TELE1 broadcaster and appointed a trustee. At the time of publication, Halk TV’s website and its social media accounts were still being run by staff while the TV station was broadcasting music and documentaries. But a court ordered all Halk TV’s social media accounts to be blocked to access from Turkey, local media reported. In a statement, the Chief Prosecutor’s Office in Istanbul said Mahiroğlu was under investigation for “bribery, collusion tendering, and laundering criminally obtained assets.” The statement said an arrest warrant had been issued for Mahiroğlu and 16 other suspects. According to the statement, companies that Mahiroğlu is a partner of or a director at, alongside companies that he has ties to, were all seized by a court order. CPJ emailed the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for comment but did not receive a reply.
